body:
How a Convex Mirror Forms an Image

A convex mirror has an outwardly curved reflecting surface. Light rays parallel to its principal axis are reflected in a diverging manner. Their backward extensions appear to originate from the principal focus F behind the mirror.

For a real object in front of a convex mirror, the reflected rays do not actually meet. Their backward extensions meet behind the reflecting surface, forming a virtual image.

A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of a real object placed in front of it.

Image Position for a Convex Mirror

Object positionImage positionSizeNature
At infinityAt F behind the mirrorHighly diminishedVirtual, erect
At any finite distance in frontBetween P and F behind the mirrorDiminishedVirtual, erect

As the object moves farther away from the mirror, its image becomes smaller and approaches the principal focus. As the object moves closer to the pole, the image becomes larger, but it remains smaller than the object for every finite object distance.

Why Convex Mirrors Are Used in Vehicles

Convex mirrors are commonly used as side or rear-view mirrors because they provide a wider field of view than a comparable plane mirror.

The outward curvature makes reflected rays diverge. As a result, a convex mirror can show a larger surrounding area within a limited mirror surface.

The image remains erect, making it convenient for the driver to recognise vehicles and other objects behind the vehicle. However, because the image is diminished, objects may appear smaller and can seem farther away than they actually are.

Other Applications

Convex mirrors are also used at some road intersections, parking areas, building exits and shop corners where a wider view helps people notice approaching vehicles or other activity.

These applications depend on the same two properties: a wide field of view and an erect, diminished virtual image.

Concave and Convex Mirrors Compared

PropertyConcave mirrorConvex mirror
Reflecting surfaceCurves inwardCurves outward
Action on parallel raysConvergesDiverges
Principal focusIn frontBehind
Image of a real objectReal or virtual, depending on positionAlways virtual
Image orientationInverted or erectAlways erect
Common applicationShaving mirror or headlight reflectorVehicle side mirror

Prelims focus

  • A convex mirror produces an erect, diminished virtual image.
  • Its principal focus lies behind the reflecting surface.
  • For a finite object distance, its image lies between P and F.
  • Convex mirrors provide a wider field of view than comparable plane mirrors.
  • Vehicle side mirrors commonly use convex reflecting surfaces.
  • Trap: A convex mirror does not form an enlarged real image of an ordinary object in front of it.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Section 9.2.2, Figure 9.8, Table 9.2 and 'Uses of convex mirrors', printed pp. 141–142.]

title: Image Formation by a Convex Mirror and Its Everyday Uses

body:
Why a Sign Convention Is Necessary

Image distances, object distances and focal lengths are measured along a chosen direction. Their algebraic signs distinguish the positions of objects and images and help describe image formation consistently.

In the New Cartesian Sign Convention, light is taken to travel from left to right toward the mirror. The pole P is the origin, and the principal axis is the horizontal reference axis.

Rules of the Sign Convention

  1. All distances parallel to the principal axis are measured from the pole P.
  2. Distances measured to the right of P, along the direction of incident light, are positive.
  3. Distances measured to the left of P, opposite the direction of incident light, are negative.
  4. Heights measured above the principal axis are positive.
  5. Heights measured below the principal axis are negative.

For the usual arrangement of a real object placed in front of the mirror, the object lies to the left and its distance u is negative.

Signs of Focal Length and Image Distance

QuantityConcave mirrorConvex mirror
Focal length fNegativePositive
Centre of curvatureIn front of mirrorBehind mirror
Real image distance vNegative when formed in frontNot formed for a real object
Virtual image distance vPositive when formed behindPositive

Mirror Formula

For a spherical mirror, let u be the signed object distance, v the signed image distance and f the signed focal length. They are related by the mirror formula:

$$\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}$$

The formula applies to both concave and convex spherical mirrors for paraxial rays, which travel close to the principal axis and make small angles with it. The correct signs must be inserted before calculation.

One-step image-distance calculation

A concave mirror has focal length -15 cm. An object is placed 30 cm in front of it.

$$u=-30\text{ cm},\quad f=-15\text{ cm}$$

$$\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f}-\frac{1}{u}=-\frac{1}{15}+\frac{1}{30}=-\frac{1}{30}$$

Therefore, \(v=-30\text{ cm}\). The image forms 30 cm in front of the mirror. It is a real image.

Magnification of a Spherical Mirror

Magnification (m) is the ratio of the signed image height to the object height. If h is the object height and h' is the image height:

$$m=\frac{h'}{h}=-\frac{v}{u}$$

The sign and magnitude of magnification describe different features of the image.

  • Positive magnification: The image is erect. For an ordinary real object in front of a spherical mirror, this corresponds to a virtual image.
  • Negative magnification: The image is inverted and real.
  • Magnitude greater than 1: The image is enlarged.
  • Magnitude equal to 1: Image and object have equal heights.
  • Magnitude less than 1: The image is diminished.

In the preceding example, \(u=-30\text{ cm}\) and \(v=-30\text{ cm}\). Therefore, \(m=-1\). The image is inverted and equal in size to the object.

For mirrors, magnification is \(m=-v/u\). The minus sign is part of the formula and must not be omitted.

Prelims focus

  • Mirror distances are measured from the pole P.
  • For a real object on the left, u is negative.
  • Concave mirror focal length is negative; convex mirror focal length is positive.
  • Mirror formula: \(1/f=1/v+1/u\).
  • Mirror magnification: \(m=-v/u\).
  • Trap: The negative sign of magnification indicates inversion, not necessarily that the image is smaller.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.2.3–9.2.4, Figure 9.9 and Examples 9.1–9.2, printed pp. 142–145; IIT Kanpur SATHEE, 'Light – Reflection and Refraction', Sections 9.2.3–9.2.4, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: From pole P, rightward distances and upward heights are positive; leftward distances and downward heights are negative, so a real object on the left has u < 0.
pictures.caption: Distances are measured from the pole, with signs determined by direction.

title: Mirror Formula, Magnification and the New Cartesian Sign Convention

body:
What Is Refraction?

Light travels at different speeds in different transparent media. When it travels obliquely from one transparent medium into another, its direction generally changes at their boundary.

Refraction of light is the change in direction of propagation of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes.

For example, a pencil partly immersed in a glass of water appears bent or displaced at the water surface. The pencil has not physically changed shape. Light from its submerged portion changes direction when it enters air, causing that portion to appear at a different position.

The Normal and the Angles of Refraction

The normal is a perpendicular drawn to the boundary at the point where the incident ray strikes it.

  • Angle of incidence (i): The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
  • Angle of refraction (r): The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.

As in reflection, both angles are measured from the normal rather than from the boundary surface.

Refraction from an Optically Rarer to a Denser Medium

When light passes obliquely from an optically rarer medium, such as air, into an optically denser medium, such as glass, its speed decreases and the ray bends toward the normal.

Under these conditions, the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence.

Refraction from an Optically Denser to a Rarer Medium

When light passes obliquely from glass into air, its speed increases and the ray bends away from the normal.

Under these conditions, the angle of refraction is larger than the angle of incidence. Above the critical angle—the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°—total internal reflection occurs instead.

Normal Incidence

If a ray enters the second medium along the normal, its angle of incidence is 0°. It continues along the same straight line without changing direction, even though its speed changes.

Refraction does not always produce a visible change in direction. At normal incidence, the ray remains undeviated despite the change in speed.

Laws of Refraction

  1. The incident ray, refracted ray and normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
  2. For a given pair of transparent media and light of a given colour, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant. This is Snell's law of refraction.

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\text{constant}$$

The constant is the refractive index of the second medium relative to the first. Snell's law applies to the ordinary transmission of light across the boundary. At normal incidence, use the equivalent relationship \(n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r\), where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the absolute refractive indices of the first and second media; both angles are then 0°.

Refraction Through a Rectangular Glass Slab

A ray passing obliquely from air into a rectangular glass slab bends toward the normal at the first surface. When it leaves the slab and enters air again, it bends away from the normal at the second surface.

Because the opposite faces of an ordinary rectangular glass slab are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the original incident ray when the medium outside both faces is the same.

However, the emergent ray is displaced sideways. This separation is called lateral displacement.

Applications and Observations

  • A coin in water appears raised because rays reaching the observer have been refracted at the water surface.
  • The bottom of a water-filled tank appears shallower than its actual depth when viewed from above.
  • A pencil partly submerged in water appears displaced at the boundary.
  • Lenses form images by refraction through their curved surfaces.

Prelims focus

  • Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes between media.
  • Rarer to denser: ray bends toward the normal.
  • Denser to rarer: ray bends away from the normal.
  • At normal incidence, there is no change in direction.
  • A rectangular glass slab produces an emergent ray parallel to the incident ray, with lateral displacement.
  • Trap: Refraction is not the same as reflection; in refraction, light passes into the second medium.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.3–9.3.1, Figure 9.10 and the laws of refraction, printed pp. 145–148.]

title: Refraction of Light: Bending at the Boundary Between Media

body:
Meaning of Refractive Index

Different transparent media affect the speed of light by different amounts. The refractive index expresses how the speed of light in a medium compares with its speed in vacuum, or how 2 media compare with each other.

The refractive index is useful because it predicts the relative bending of a light ray at a boundary between transparent materials.

Absolute Refractive Index

The absolute refractive index of a transparent medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium.

$$n=\frac{c}{v}$$

Here, n is the absolute refractive index, c is the speed of light in vacuum and v is the speed of light in the medium.

The approximate speed of light in vacuum is:

$$c=3\times10^8\text{ m/s}$$

Because refractive index is a ratio of 2 speeds, it has no unit.

Relative Refractive Index

Suppose light travels from medium 1 into medium 2. Let its speeds in these media be v1 and v2.

The refractive index of medium 2 relative to medium 1 is:

$$n_{21}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

For ordinary refraction, this relative index is also expressed through Snell's law as:

$$n_{21}=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}$$

These expressions apply to light of a specified colour and the given pair of media.

Approximate Refractive Indices of Common Materials

Refractive index depends on the material and the wavelength of light. The following are representative textbook values for visible light.

MediumApproximate refractive indexOptical comparison
Air1.0003Nearly the same as vacuum
Water1.33Denser than air
Kerosene1.44Denser than water
Crown glass1.52Denser than water
Diamond2.42Very high refractive index

These are illustrative material values, not universal constants for every colour, glass composition or condition.

Connection Between Refractive Index and Speed

For 2 transparent media, the medium with a greater refractive index has a lower speed of light for the specified wavelength comparison.

For example, a material with refractive index 1.5 has an approximate light speed:

$$v=\frac{3\times10^8}{1.5}=2\times10^8\text{ m/s}$$

Thus, light travels more slowly in this material than in vacuum.

Optical Density and Mass Density Are Different

A medium with a higher refractive index is called optically denser than a medium with a lower refractive index. The terms optically denser and optically rarer describe the effect of a material on light, not the amount of mass contained in a given volume.

For example, kerosene has a higher refractive index than water: approximately 1.44 compared with 1.33. Therefore, kerosene is optically denser than water, even though ordinary kerosene has a lower mass density than water.

Predicting Bending from Refractive Index

If light enters a medium with a higher refractive index, its speed decreases and an oblique ray bends toward the normal.

If light enters a medium with a lower refractive index, its speed increases and an oblique ray bends away from the normal.

The extent of bending also depends on the angle of incidence. At normal incidence, no angular deviation occurs.

Higher refractive index means lower light speed in the corresponding medium and greater optical density. It does not necessarily mean greater mass density.

Prelims focus

  • Absolute refractive index: \(n=c/v\).
  • Relative refractive index: \(n_{21}=v_1/v_2\).
  • Refractive index is dimensionless.
  • Approximate values: water 1.33, crown glass 1.52 and diamond 2.42.
  • A higher refractive index corresponds to lower light speed.
  • Trap: Optical density must not be confused with mass density.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Section 9.3.2, Equations 9.4–9.7 and Table 9.3, printed pp. 148–150.]

pictures.caption: Optical density and mass density do not necessarily follow the same order.

title: Refractive Index, Speed of Light and Optical Density
